science.title: Low-frequency jet ventilation as a form of pressure-controlled ventilation: a mechanistic study using simulated lung models
science.description: Jet ventilation requires an open airway, making accurate monitoring of tidal volume (VT) and airway pressure (Paw) challenging. Whether low frequency jet ventilation (LFJV) is comparable to conventional pressure-controlled ventilation (PCV) in terms of VT, pressure rise time (Tslope), and pressure rise slope (Ramp) remains unclear due to limited evidence. Using two simulated lung models under open airway conditions, LFJV and PCV were compared. The LFJV group was ventilated with a driving pressure (DP) of 0.6–1.6 bar, frequency of 10–30 bpm, and I: E ratio of 1:1. VT, peak inspiratory pressure (PIP), and machine delivered flow (Flowinject) were measured, with Paw waveforms recorded. In the PCV group, PIP values from the LFJV group were used as the target inspiratory pressure (Pinsp), with matching frequency and I: E ratio, while using the default inspiratory flow (Flowinsp) of 30 L/min. Tslope and Ramp were derived from Paw waveforms in both groups. VT did not differ significantly between the two groups (mean difference: − 43.03 mL [95% CI: − 123.58 to 37.53], P = 0.2925). Machine-delivered flow (Flowinject in LFJV vs. Flowinsp in PCV) also showed no significant difference (mean difference: 0.6 L/min [95% CI: − 7.25 to 8.45], P = 0.8520). The Tslope was significantly shorter in the LFJV group than in the PCV group (mean difference: − 0.58 s [95% CI: − 0.96 to − 0.20], P = 0.0066), and the Ramp was markedly steeper in LFJV (mean difference: 23.7 cmH₂O/s [95% CI: 18.25 to 29.16], P < 0.0001). Low-frequency jet ventilation can be characterized as a pressure-controlled mode under the conditions tested, whose pressurization kinetics are directly governed by driving pressure. The preserved acceleration in pressure rise, even at matched machine-delivered flows, highlights the unique role of Venturi-augmented flow in LFJV’s gas delivery dynamics.

science.title: A backpressure-driven flow control model for stabilizing MQTT communication in IoT systems
science.description: This paper investigates the stability challenges of the Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) protocol in Internet of Things (IoT) environments under varying traffic loads and network conditions. While MQTT is widely adopted for its lightweight design and efficiency, it lacks effective application-level flow-control mechanisms, which can lead to broker congestion, increased latency, and message loss when publishing rates exceed the effective processing capacity of the experimental communication pipeline. This study demonstrates that a lightweight backpressure-driven adaptive flow-control mechanism can substantially improve MQTT communication stability under controlled experimental conditions. The approach dynamically adjusts the message transmission rate based on real-time system indicators, including end-to-end latency, delivery success rate, and congestion signals. Unlike existing approaches that rely on static configurations or simulation-based evaluations, this study employs a controlled experimental testbed using an Eclipse Mosquitto broker and C + + MQTT clients to compare default MQTT behavior with adaptive publishing under normal, high-load, and adverse network conditions. Experimental results from the baseline MQTT configuration without adaptive control demonstrate that uncontrolled publishing leads to queue buildup, significant latency growth, and reduced delivery reliability as system load increases. In contrast, the proposed adaptive mechanism effectively regulates message rates, reduces congestion effects, and maintains more stable throughput and higher delivery success rates. Statistical validation confirms that improvements are significant (p < 0.01). These findings indicate that application-layer flow control can significantly enhance MQTT communication stability without requiring modifications to the protocol or broker implementation, making it suitable for practical IoT deployments.

science.title: Quantum chemical, spectroscopic, and in silico molecular docking and molecular dynamics studies on thymotrinan, which has immunomodulatory and neuroprotective properties
science.description: Thymotrinan is an immunomodulating tripeptide containing the Arg-Lys-Asp sequence.In this study, the structural, vibrational, and electronic properties, as well as the bioactivity of thymotrinan, have been thoroughly examined.The conformational preferences of thymotrinan were evaluated through conformational analysis, and the lowest-energy conformer was then optimized using DFT/WB97XD/6–31 + + G(d, p) theory level.The vibrational wavenumbers of the optimized structure were calculated, and the molecular electrostatic potential (MEP) and frontier molecular orbital (HOMO, LUMO) analyses were performed. To analyze how thymotrinan interacts with the α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor chimera and to evaluate its potential to inhibit α-Bungarotoxin, a snake venom protein, molecular docking studies were performed between thymotrinan and target proteins, including the α7nAchR chimera in complex with α-BTx(PDB ID 4HQP), the α7nAchR chimera without the α-BTx protein(α-BTx-removed 4HQP), and α-BTx(PDB code: 1IK8).Afterwards, the thymotrinan-1IK8 complex was subjected to 200 ns of all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to demonstrate its stability.Based on the MD trajectory, the binding free energy of the complex was estimated to be -18.545 kcal/mol using the MM-PBSA method.In addition, in silico pharmacological predictions suggest that thymotrinan may exhibit anticancer activity against multiple cancer cell lines and antibacterial activity against a range of bacterial species. However, experimental validation of these findings remains required.
